```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
library(bayesnec)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
```

## Background

The posterior draws a Bayesian fit produces are useful well beyond a point
estimate. They support the study of synergistic and antagonistic effects
[@Fisher2019d; @flores2021], the propagation of endpoint uncertainty
[@Charles2020a; @Gottschalk2013], and tests of hypotheses of no effect
[@Thomas2006].

`compare_posterior()` uses them to compare fits: differences in a threshold
estimate such as the *NEC*, *NSEC* or an **EC~x~**, or differences across a
range of predictor values.

```{r}
#| label: fig-context
#| out-width: "48%"
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(c("images/dredging_effects.JPG", "images/herbicides_climate.JPG"))
```

## The data

Earlier modules used simulated data. This one works through a real analysis:
estimating no-effect concentrations for a set of herbicides and comparing their
relative toxicity.

The data are from @jones2003meps and ship with `bayesnec`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-source
#| out-width: "48%"
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(c("images/jonesnkerswell.jpg", "images/s_hystrix.jpg"))
```

The response is the maximum effective quantum yield, $\Delta F / Fm'$, of
symbiotic dinoflagellates in the tissue of the coral *Seriatopora hystrix*,
calculated from chlorophyll fluorescence measured with a DIVING-PAM fluorometer
[@jones2003meps; @jones2003effects]. Corals were exposed for 10 hours to eight
herbicides at concentrations from 0.3 to 1000 $\mu g L^{-1}$. Ioxynil is
excluded here because it produced no adequate response at the highest
concentration, leaving seven.

```{r}
#| label: data
data(herbicide)
str(herbicide)
table(herbicide$herbicide)
```

## Provenance of these fits

Seven herbicides fitted against the `decline` set is
`r length(models()$decline)` equations each, and takes hours. These fits are
therefore **not run when this page is built**. They are produced by
`scripts/generate_herbicide_fits.R`, which writes the compact results this
module reads. The fitted objects themselves are far too large to keep — the
2023 equivalent was 451 MB.

The code shown below is the code that was run. It is displayed rather than
executed, and every result on this page comes from that run.

```{r}
#| label: provenance
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
cat(readLines("data/herbicide_provenance.txt"), sep = "\n")
```

## A single herbicide

Taking ametryn first. The concentration is log transformed before fitting, both
because it stabilises the fit and because the concentration series is
logarithmic by design. There is little evidence of hormesis in these data, so
the `decline` set is used rather than the full set.

```{r}
#| label: fit-ametryn-shown
#| eval: false
ametryn <- herbicide |>
  mutate(concentration = log(concentration)) |>
  filter(herbicide == "ametryn")

manecfit_ametryn <- bnec(fvfm ~ crf(concentration, model = "decline"),
                         data = ametryn, seed = 17)
```

Every argument other than the model set is left at its default. `bayesnec`
selects a beta distribution for the response, uses the identity link, and drops
`neclin` and `ecxlin` from the `decline` set because they are not suitable for a
zero-bounded distribution.

### The summary

```{r}
#| label: ametryn-summary
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
cat(readLines("data/ametryn_summary.txt"), sep = "\n")
```

The weights are spread across several smooth equations with limited support for
the threshold models. The no-effect estimate is reported on the log
concentration scale, because that is the scale the model was fitted on.

### Every equation in the set

```{r}
#| label: fig-ametryn-all
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Each equation fitted to the ametryn data, with its 95% credible interval."
allmods <- read.csv("data/ametryn_allmodels.csv")

ggplot(allmods, aes(x = concentration)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Q2.5, ymax = Q97.5), fill = "grey80") +
  geom_line(aes(y = Estimate)) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log",
                     breaks = c(0.3, 3, 30, 300)) +
  labs(x = expression("Concentration ("*mu*"g/L)"),
       y = expression(Delta*"F/Fm'")) +
  theme_classic()
```

Fits should also be checked with `check_chains()` and `check_priors()`, as
modules 4 and 6 describe. Both take a `filename`, which writes the plots to a
PDF suitable for an analysis appendix rather than to the screen.

## The complete set of herbicides

The same call is applied to each herbicide in turn.

```{r}
#| label: fit-all-shown
#| eval: false
manecfit <- herbicide |>
  mutate(concentration = log(concentration)) |>
  split(f = ~ herbicide) |>
  purrr::map(function(x) {
    bnec(fvfm ~ crf(concentration, model = "decline"), data = x, seed = 17)
  })
```

### Screening the model sets

Each of the seven sets is screened on all three sampler diagnostics before it is
used, as module 4 describes.

```{r}
#| label: clean-shown
#| eval: false
sampling <- purrr::imap_dfr(manecfit, function(fit, nm) {
  check_sampling(fit) |> mutate(herbicide = nm, .before = 1)
})

cleaned_fits <- purrr::map(manecfit, screen_models)
```

`screen_models()` drops the equations that failed and reports which went and why.
Do not reach for `rhat(fit)$failed` in its place: `rhat()` on a `bayesmanecfit`
returns a list keyed by model name, each element holding the R-hat values and a
logical `failed`, so `$failed` on the list itself is `NULL` and silently drops
nothing. The earlier version of this module had that defect.

The full table is kept rather than only the failures, because the thresholds
applied are part of what has to be reported:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sampling
#| tbl-cap: "Sampler diagnostics for every fitted equation, with the models the screen removed marked in the final column."
sampling <- read.csv("data/herbicide_sampling.csv")

sampling |>
  summarise(equations = dplyr::n(),
            removed = sum(failed),
            .by = herbicide) |>
  kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-screened
#| echo: false
removed <- subset(sampling, failed)
if (nrow(removed) == 0) {
  cat("No equation failed the sampler screen.\n")
} else {
  removed |>
    transmute(Herbicide = herbicide, Model = model,
              `Max R-hat` = signif(max_rhat, 4),
              `Min ESS` = round(min_ess),
              Divergences = n_divergent) |>
    kable(caption = "Equations removed by the screen, and the diagnostic each failed.")
}
```

Equations that produced no draws at all are a different failure, and are reported
separately by `failed_models()`:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-neverfit
#| echo: false
nf <- read.csv("data/herbicide_never_fitted.csv")
if (nrow(nf) == 0) {
  cat("Every requested equation produced draws.\n")
} else {
  kable(nf, caption = "Equations that failed to fit at all.")
}
```

Module 4 sets out why the two are worth separating: an equation short of draws
needs more of them, while an equation the design cannot support needs reporting
as excluded.

## Model weights across herbicides

```{r}
#| label: tbl-weights
#| tbl-cap: "Fitted models and their relative weights, for the effect of seven herbicides on the maximum effective quantum yield of symbiotic dinoflagellates of *Seriatopora hystrix*."
modstats <- read.csv("data/herbicide_mod_stats.csv")

modstats |>
  mutate(wi = round(wi, 3)) |>
  select(herbicide, model, wi) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = herbicide, values_from = wi) |>
  kable()
```

The best-fitting equations differ substantially between herbicides. Few show
much weight on the threshold models. Among the smooth equations the weights vary
widely, with support for more than one in every case.

That is the argument for model averaging in a sentence: there is no single
equation that is right for these data, the best one differs by herbicide, and
selecting one would discard the uncertainty about which. Averaging propagates it
into the estimates instead.

Some models failed to fit under the default settings for every herbicide. Custom
priors or initial values would likely recover them, but with a large number of
well-fitting models already in each set, doing so is unlikely to change the
inference.

## The fitted curves

```{r}
#| label: fig-all-herbicides
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Model-averaged concentration-response curves for seven herbicides, with 95% credible intervals and the observations."
preds <- read.csv("data/herbicide_pred_vals.csv")
obs   <- read.csv("data/herbicide_observations.csv")

ggplot(preds, aes(x = concentration)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Q2.5, ymax = Q97.5), fill = "grey80") +
  geom_line(aes(y = Estimate)) +
  geom_point(data = obs, aes(y = fvfm), size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ herbicide, ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log", breaks = c(0.3, 3, 30, 300)) +
  labs(x = expression("Concentration ("*mu*"g/L)"),
       y = expression(Delta*"F/Fm'")) +
  theme_classic()
```

## The toxicity estimates

The value reported for each herbicide is a model-averaged posterior combining
the *NEC* parameter from the threshold equations with the *NSEC* from the smooth
ones, which is what module 3 described. It is labelled N(S)EC for that reason.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-estimates
#| tbl-cap: "Model-averaged no-effect estimates, back-transformed to concentration."
read.csv("data/herbicide_estimates.csv") |>
  transmute(Herbicide = herbicide,
            `Estimate` = signif(estimate, 3),
            `Lower 95%` = signif(lower, 3),
            `Upper 95%` = signif(upper, 3)) |>
  kable()
```

These are the estimates that would enter a guideline derivation. In Australia
that is the Australian and New Zealand Water Quality Guidelines [@anzg]. The
*NEC* has been the established preference for some time [@Warne2015; @warne2018],
and the 2025 revision of the derivation method [@warne2025] places the *NSEC*
alongside it: the two are now the most preferred statistical estimates, with an
**EC~x~** at *x* of 10 or less in the tier below them.

That has a practical consequence for a table like the one above. Because the
*NSEC* sits in the preferred tier, the condition attached to it applies, and an
*NSEC* whose measured effect size exceeds 20% should probably not be used to
derive a guideline value. Module 3 covers the ECNSEC, which is the quantity that
measures it, and an analysis reporting an N(S)EC for guideline use should report
that alongside.

```{r}
#| label: fig-nsecieam
#| out-width: "34%"
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics("images/NSEC_ieam.jpg")
```

## Comparing the posteriors

`compare_posterior()` extracts the weighted posterior for each fit so they can
be compared directly, rather than by asking whether intervals overlap.

`comparison` names the quantity compared, and takes `"nec"`, `"n(s)ec"`,
`"nsec"`, `"ecx"` or `"fitted"`. `"n(s)ec"` is used here because these sets mix
threshold and smooth equations, so the weighted no-effect posterior is a mixture
of both kinds of estimate. Asking for `"nec"` would compare the threshold
parameter alone, over the equations that have one, which is a different quantity
and would be a different table.

```{r}
#| label: compare-shown
#| eval: false
post_comp <- compare_posterior(cleaned_fits, comparison = "n(s)ec")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-posteriors
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Posterior densities of the N(S)EC estimate for each herbicide."
post <- read.csv("data/herbicide_ne_posterior.csv")

ggplot(post, aes(x = concentration, group = model,
                 colour = model, fill = model)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.3) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log", breaks = c(0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30),
                     labels = c(0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30)) +
  labs(x = expression("Concentration ("*mu*"g/L)"), y = "Density",
       colour = "Herbicide", fill = "Herbicide") +
  theme_classic()
```

Irgarol, diuron and ametryn are the most toxic and are similar to one another,
their densities overlapping substantially. Tebuthiuron is the least toxic,
followed by simazine and atrazine, with hexazinone intermediate.

## Probabilities of difference

Overlapping densities are a visual impression. `compare_posterior()` also
returns the probability that one estimate is lower than another, computed from
the draws.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-probdiff
#| tbl-cap: "Probability of difference in no-effect toxicity between herbicides, from the overlap in their posterior densities."
read.csv("data/herbicide_prob_diff.csv") |>
  separate(col = comparison, into = c("herbicide", "against"), sep = "-") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = against, values_from = prob) |>
  kable()
```

This is the practical advantage of having the posterior rather than an interval.
The question of whether A is more toxic than B is answered with a probability
computed from the draws, without a significance test, and it propagates the
uncertainty in the curve shape as well as in the parameters.

## The parameters behind the estimates

`summary()` reports the weights and the no-effect estimate and no parameter
estimates at all. `curve_params()` returns those, one row per parameter per
equation, with the model weight beside each row:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-curveparams
#| tbl-cap: "Fitted curve parameters for ametryn, with the weight of the equation each came from."
read.csv("data/herbicide_curve_params.csv") |>
  filter(herbicide == "ametryn") |>
  transmute(Model = model, Parameter = parameter,
            Estimate = signif(Estimate, 3),
            `Lower 95%` = signif(Q2.5, 3),
            `Upper 95%` = signif(Q97.5, 3),
            Weight = round(wi, 3)) |>
  kable()
```

Nothing is averaged across the equations, because they do not share a parameter
list: only the threshold equations estimate `nec`, and the three-parameter
equations have no `bot`. Averaging a parameter over whichever equations happen to
estimate it would average over a different subset of the set for each parameter.
The weight beside each row is what makes the table readable, since a row holding
a thousandth of the weight describes the averaged curve hardly at all.

`xform = exp` was applied when these were generated, and it reaches `nec` and
`ec50` and no other parameter, because those two are on the predictor axis while
`top`, `bot` and `beta` are levels of the response or shape parameters.

## Reporting the analysis

The estimates above are the output. What follows is what has to accompany them,
because almost every number in this module is a property of a decision as much as
of the data.

State **the data as analysed**: the response, the bounds of its distribution, and
any value altered to bring it inside the family's support. `bnec_record()`
reports the last of these in its `substitutions` element.

State **the family and how it was chosen**. Here `bayesnec` inferred a beta
distribution from a continuous response bounded by 0 and 1. For a count out of a
total, report the dispersion screen of module 5 and the probability it returned.

State **the candidate set as fitted**: the set requested, the equations excluded
before fitting and why, and any equation that failed to fit at all.
`bnec_record()` returns the first three and `failed_models()` the last.

State **the sampler settings**, including the number of retained draws rather
than `iter` alone, because two of the three diagnostic cutoffs are absolute
counts read against them.

State **the diagnostic thresholds**, all three of them. They are choices, they
determine what was excluded, and `check_sampling()` allows each to be changed.

State **which equations were excluded and why**, naming the threshold each
failed, and distinguishing an equation that would pass with more draws from one
the design cannot support.

State **the estimate settings**: `sig_val`, which sets the *NSEC* reference and
defaults to 0.01; `type`, which sets what an **EC~x~** is measured against and
defaults to `"absolute"`; `resolution`, the number of grid points a crossing is
interpolated on, which defaults to 200; and any `xform` used to return an
estimate to the measured scale.

State **the estimates with their intervals and the weights** of the retained
equations, and **the parameters of the fitted curve** that the estimates were
read from.

One of those deserves emphasis here because this analysis was fitted on a
transformed predictor. Every estimate is returned on the scale it was fitted on
unless `xform` says otherwise, and a logged value can land in the same numeric
range as a concentration and pass unremarked. Reporting a logged value as a
concentration understates the threshold by a factor of e for every unit on the
logged scale, and only a negative logarithm announces the error. A reported value
has to state the scale it is on.
